title: Medicare Cost Savings 2027: New CMS Billing Rules

sections.text: What's Changing with Medicare Costs in 2027

sections.content: The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) has finalized policy updates designed to lower what you pay out of pocket for certain outpatient imaging services, like MRIs and CT scans, along with specific outpatient drugs covered under Medicare Part B. These changes are aimed at reducing coinsurance costs and making your medical bills easier to predict ahead of time.

It helps to know the timing here. These updates take effect in 2027, not right away, so your 2026 costs for imaging and Part B drugs remain exactly as they are today. Nothing changes on your current bills this year.

CMS has framed this adjustment as a response to growing patient cost-sharing on high-cost outpatient services. The goal is simpler and more consistent billing, so you have a clearer sense of what a scan or infusion will actually cost before you receive care.

Coinsurance on outpatient imaging and Part B drugs has been rising for years, and for many beneficiaries, a single MRI or infusion visit can carry a cost-sharing bill that is hard to anticipate. Under standard Medicare Part B, you typically pay 20% coinsurance after meeting your deductible, and that percentage can translate into very different dollar amounts depending on the total charge for the service.

CMS is addressing this by adjusting how payment and cost-sharing are calculated for these specific services, not by reducing what Medicare covers. The services themselves remain covered benefits; what changes is the formula behind your share of the cost.

This update is part of a larger pattern of CMS reviewing high-cost outpatient categories for affordability concerns, consistent with its ongoing work on Medicare payment policy published through annual rule updates at [CMS.gov](https://www.cms.gov/).

sections.text: How the Changes Affect Imaging Services

sections.content: The 2027 changes apply to a defined set of outpatient diagnostic imaging services commonly ordered to evaluate conditions like joint pain, cardiac issues, or cancer staging. These include:

items: Certain advanced diagnostic imaging performed in outpatient settings

sections.content: If you receive imaging through a hospital outpatient department rather than an independent imaging center, you may notice the largest cost difference, since hospital outpatient billing has historically carried higher cost-sharing under Part B.

sections.text: What You Might Notice on Your Bill

sections.content: Instead of paying a straight 20% coinsurance on the full charge for a scan, the new structure moves toward standardized, capped cost-sharing amounts for included imaging services. This means your share is less dependent on the total billed amount and more predictable regardless of which outpatient facility performs the scan.

As a simple illustration: if an MRI currently results in a coinsurance bill of around $300 under standard 20% cost-sharing, a capped structure might bring that same service down to a lower, fixed amount once the 2027 rule applies. This is a hypothetical example to show the shift in structure, not a confirmed dollar figure, since CMS has not published final capped amounts for every service.

sections.calloutText: Once the 2027 changes take effect, compare the coinsurance line items on your Medicare Summary Notice against prior statements for the same type of service. This is the clearest way to see the real dollar impact on your own bills.

sections.text: How the Changes Affect Outpatient Drug Costs
Which Drugs Are Covered Under This Change

sections.content: This part of the update applies specifically to Part B drugs, meaning medications administered in a clinical setting such as a doctor's office or outpatient infusion center. It does not apply to Part D prescription drugs you pick up at a pharmacy.

Common examples include chemotherapy infusions and biologic injectables given during an office visit. These drugs are typically billed differently than retail prescriptions, with cost-sharing tied to the Part B deductible and coinsurance structure rather than a Part D copay tier.

How much you might save depends heavily on which drug you receive and how often you need treatment. A single annual infusion will see a smaller cumulative benefit than a drug administered weekly or monthly, since the adjusted cost-sharing applies per claim.

If you have supplemental coverage, such as a Medigap plan, your out-of-pocket responsibility may already be reduced for Part B coinsurance, which means the practical effect of this federal change could look different depending on your existing coverage. It's worth understanding both pieces together rather than assuming the new rule is the only factor at play.

If you're weighing whether to adjust your coverage before 2027, don't make that decision based on this policy alone. Look at your full picture first, including your current Medigap or Medicare Advantage cost-sharing for imaging and infusions, since the federal change may simply layer on top of protections you already have.

sections.text: What to Watch for in Your Future Medicare Billing Statements

sections.content: Once the 2027 rules are active, a little routine review can help you confirm the savings are actually showing up and catch any billing mistakes early. Consider these steps each time you receive a statement for imaging or an outpatient drug claim:

items: Review your Medicare Summary Notice for updated coinsurance amounts tied to imaging or Part B drug claims.
Compare the new costs against prior statements from the same provider for a similar service.
Confirm your provider has updated their billing codes to reflect the new payment structure.
Contact Medicare or your plan directly if a charge looks incorrect or doesn't match what you expected.

sections.content: This kind of regular check is useful beyond just tracking savings. Reviewing your statements closely is one of the most reliable ways to catch a billing error before it becomes a larger dispute, something the [Medicare Summary Notice](https://www.medicare.gov/) is specifically designed to help you do.

sections.text: How These Changes Fit Into Your Overall Medicare Planning

sections.content: A federal payment change like this is a good prompt to revisit your broader coverage choices, particularly during your next opportunity to review Medigap or Medicare Advantage options. Since cost-sharing formulas are shifting for specific services, it's worth asking whether your current plan still matches how you use imaging and outpatient drug services.

Not every plan will see the same benefit from these changes. Medicare Advantage plans set their own cost-sharing structures within federal guidelines, so the practical savings from this update could look different depending on your specific plan's existing rules for imaging and infusions.

A licensed Medicare agent can help translate what this federal policy update means for your specific coverage, since they can look at your plan's current cost-sharing rules alongside these new CMS changes.

faqs.question: Do I need to do anything right now to benefit from these 2027 changes?
faqs.answer: No action is needed yet. The changes don't begin until 2027, so your best step for now is to keep your current coverage in place and start reviewing your Medicare Summary Notices more closely once the updates roll out, so you can confirm the new cost-sharing amounts are being applied correctly.

faqs.question: Will someone try to sell me a new plan because of this policy update?
faqs.answer: This is a federal payment policy change, not a signal that you need to switch plans immediately. If you do seek guidance on how it affects your coverage, that conversation should come from a licensed agent who explains your options clearly, without pressure to enroll in anything new right away.

faqs.question: Can I just read more about this later and decide if it affects me?
faqs.answer: Yes, taking time to understand how this applies to your situation is reasonable, especially since the changes aren't effective until 2027. Official updates from CMS.gov and trustworthy Medicare resources will remain available as ongoing references as implementation details are finalized.

faqs.question: How do I know if this information is accurate and not outdated?
faqs.answer: CMS policy details can be refined before the 2027 implementation date, so figures and specifics may shift slightly. The most reliable approach is to check official announcements directly on [CMS.gov](https://www.cms.gov/) and cross-reference with reputable Medicare resources for the latest confirmed information as the date approaches.

sections.text: Your Next Step Toward Lower Medicare Costs

sections.content: These 2027 changes are meant to ease the financial strain of outpatient imaging and certain Part B drug costs, and they don't require you to act immediately. What they do offer is a window of time to look closely at your current coverage and ask questions before the new cost-sharing rules take effect.

Use this period to review how your plan currently handles imaging and infusion costs, and consider whether your coverage still fits your needs. If you'd like a clearer picture of how these updates may apply to your specific situation, a [licensed Medicare agent](/medicare-supplement-plans/plan-g/) can walk through your plan with you, with no pressure to make changes before you're ready.

seoDescription: Medicare cost savings 2027: CMS caps coinsurance on imaging and Part B drugs to make your bills more predictable. See what changes and when.
excerpt: CMS has finalized 2027 changes that cap coinsurance for certain outpatient imaging and Part B drugs, aiming to make costs more predictable. Your 2026 bills stay the same.
keyTakeaways: CMS finalized new rules capping coinsurance for select outpatient imaging services (MRIs, CT scans) and Part B drugs starting in 2027
No changes apply in 2026; current cost-sharing rules remain in effect until the new policy takes effect
The update changes how cost-sharing is calculated, not what Medicare covers, moving toward standardized, capped amounts instead of straight 20% coinsurance
Hospital outpatient imaging may see the biggest cost difference since it historically carries higher cost-sharing than independent imaging centers
CMS has not yet published final capped dollar amounts for every affected service
